lead: Gilbert grew from a farm town into a city of about 280,000 in a few decades. Its 2000s homes are now hitting the age when roofs, water heaters and softeners start to fail.
risk: aging tile roof underlayment, monsoon storms and garage water heater leaks
why: Most Gilbert homes are young; the median year built is 2003. But young is not new anymore. Many of those houses have concrete tile roofs. The tiles last for decades, but the felt underlayment beneath them often wears out after about 20 years. When it cracks, monsoon rain gets past the tiles and into the attic. The leak may only show up as a ceiling stain weeks later.

Gilbert also has a high share of owner-occupied homes, 73%, and lots of home equipment. Water softeners, reverse osmosis units and garage water heaters all have hoses and valves that wear out, and the Valley's hard water speeds that up. In summer, AC units in the attic drip constantly. A clogged condensate line can overflow and soak the ceiling below.
image_alt: Ceiling damaged by a slow roof leak in a Gilbert-area home
image_caption: Worn tile roof underlayment can let monsoon rain into Gilbert attics.
problems: 2000s homes in Power Ranch, Seville, Morrison Ranch
tips: Have a tile roof's underlayment checked once the house hits 15 to 20 years.
Flush the AC condensate line with vinegar before summer.
Put a leak alarm next to the water heater and softener.
Keep yard drains and retention basins clear of debris.
areas: Calls come from the Heritage District, Agritopia, Val Vista Lakes, Power Ranch, Seville, Morrison Ranch, Lyons Gate and Finley Farms, plus Queen Creek and San Tan Valley.

faq.q: Why is my Gilbert tile roof leaking if the tiles look fine?
faq.a: Concrete tiles shed most water, but the underlayment beneath them is the real barrier. In the Arizona heat it can crack and break down after about 20 years. Rain then slips under the tiles and into the attic. A roofer can lift tiles and replace the underlayment.
